lead: This unit is about protecting cloud workloads, data and identities across shared infrastructure. You learn to name threats, choose controls, follow data through its lifecycle, and respond when controls fail. After it, you can reason about a cloud security design and answer exam questions with clear mechanisms and trade-offs.
about: This unit turns cloud security from a list of fears into a set of controls. Chapter 6.1 maps threats and attack paths. 6.2 gives the four security services, and 6.3 shows how encryption and keys deliver confidentiality and integrity. 6.4 follows data through retention and deletion. 6.5 covers IAM, while 6.6 adds MFA, SSO and federation. 6.7 explains VM isolation, and 6.8 applies patterns to cloud bursting and secure interfaces. 6.9 closes with monitoring, auditing and incident response. The chapters build from risk to service goals, then to data, identity, runtime isolation and operations.

chapters.idea: Cloud security is a shared job: the provider protects the platform, the customer protects identities, configurations and data, and every exposed interface adds an attack path.
chapters.depth: Define threat, vulnerability, risk and attack vector. Cover credential theft, misconfigured storage, insecure APIs, DDoS, co-residency, insider abuse and supply chain. Map each to the network, storage or identity layer. Use the shared responsibility model and attack surface. Mention STRIDE only as a checklist.

figure.title: One attack path
figure.aria: A four-step attack path from weak identity controls to a stolen key, a public bucket holding 10,000 records, and a data breach.

chapters.example: A public bucket holds 10,000 customer records. A stolen key gives read access. Asset value is ₹50,00,000, exposure factor is 0.4, and two such incidents happen a year. Find the single loss expectancy (SLE) and annual loss expectancy (ALE). SLE = ₹50,00,000 × 0.4 = ₹20,00,000. ALE = ₹20,00,000 × 2 = ₹40,00,000.
chapters.trap: A threat is not a risk, and a vulnerability is not an attack. The provider secures physical hosts, but the customer still owns bucket policy, IAM and data classification.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: NIST cloud definition and service models; Unit 2: web APIs and networks.
chapters.leave: Control details go to 6.2 to 6.9; virtualization threats go to 6.7.

chapters.idea: Confidentiality, integrity, authentication and non-repudiation are four security goals, each with its own mechanism and its own cloud failure mode.
chapters.depth: Some syllabi call this the CIA triad plus authentication and non-repudiation. Define each service. Confidentiality uses encryption and access control. Integrity uses hashes, MACs and authenticated encryption. Authentication uses passwords, keys or MFA. Non-repudiation uses digital signatures and audit logs. Distinguish authentication from authorization. Mention availability as the A in CIA.

figure.aria: A tree with security services at the root and confidentiality, integrity, authentication and non-repudiation as four branches with their mechanisms.

chapters.example: A ₹10,000 UPI payment is protected in four ways. The app encrypts the PIN for confidentiality. The bank checks a message authentication code for integrity. The phone unlock plus UPI PIN authenticates the user. A signed bank log supports non-repudiation. If the amount is changed from ₹10,000 to ₹1,000 in transit, which service fails? Integrity.
chapters.trap: Encryption gives confidentiality, not integrity by itself. A plain hash gives integrity but not authentication unless it is keyed or signed. Authentication is not non-repudiation.
chapters.leave: Encryption and key management go to 6.3; IAM to 6.5; MFA, SSO and federation to 6.6.

chapters.idea: Cloud encryption protects data at rest and in transit, but its strength depends on the key hierarchy, key custody and key lifecycle.
chapters.depth: Compare symmetric AES with asymmetric RSA and ECC. Cover TLS for data in transit, envelope encryption, KMS and HSM, data encryption keys (DEKs), key encryption keys (KEKs) and root keys. Include rotation, revocation, escrow, BYOK and HYOK. Add PKI certificates and certificate chains. Note that tokenization is not encryption and is covered in 6.4.

figure.title: Key hierarchy
figure.aria: A key hierarchy from a root key in an HSM, to a tenant key-encryption key that wraps 1,000 data encryption keys, to 1,000 encrypted objects.

chapters.example: A tenant has 1,000 objects. Each object has its own 256-bit data encryption key (DEK). One tenant key-encryption key (KEK) wraps all 1,000 DEKs. Rotating the KEK rewraps 1,000 DEKs. How many object re-encryptions are needed? Zero.
chapters.trap: A key stored beside the ciphertext gives no protection. Rotating a KEK does not re-encrypt data; rotating a DEK does. Encryption alone does not prove integrity unless authenticated encryption or a MAC is used.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 confidentiality and integrity; Unit 2 TLS and web services.
chapters.leave: Data retention to 6.4; key access control to 6.5.

chapters.idea: Data protection follows the data lifecycle: classify it, control access, encrypt or redact when needed, retain only as long as required, then delete or archive safely.
chapters.depth: Cover data classification, DLP, encryption, tokenization, redaction and obfuscation. Explain retention policies, legal hold, archiving, deletion and backup expiry. Include tenant data separation and secure disposal. Contrast retention with backup lifetime.

figure.aria: A retention timeline for logs: 90 days active at 900 GB, archive from day 90 to day 365 at 275 GB, then a purge window.

chapters.example: A service writes 10 GB of logs per day. Logs stay active for 90 days. Then they are archived with 10:1 compression until day 365. A purge runs from day 365 to day 370. Storage at day 364: active = 10 × 90 = 900 GB. Archive raw = 10 × 275 = 2,750 GB; compressed = 2,750 ÷ 10 = 275 GB. Total = 900 + 275 = 1,175 GB. After purge, 0 GB.
chapters.trap: Deleting the live copy is not deletion if backups, snapshots or replicas still hold it. Retention is a policy, not just storage lifetime; legal hold can override deletion.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 cloud storage, replication and backups; 6.3 encryption.
chapters.leave: Access control to 6.5; audit logs to 6.9.

chapters.idea: IAM decides which authenticated principal may perform which action on which resource under which conditions.
chapters.depth: Cover identities, users, groups, roles, service accounts and policies. Explain RBAC and ABAC, least privilege, separation of duties, allow and deny evaluation, temporary credentials, cross-account trust and privilege escalation. Keep federation, SSO and MFA for 6.6.

figure.aria: A decision tree for a request: MFA must pass, the source IP must be in range, and the role must allow the action; any failure leads to deny.

chapters.example: Role Analyst has an allow policy for read on finance data when MFA is present and the source IP is in 10.0.0.0/8. Request A: MFA yes, IP 10.1.2.3, role allows → Allow. Request B: MFA yes, IP 192.168.1.5 → Deny. Request C: no MFA → Deny.
chapters.trap: Authentication says who you are; IAM authorization says what you can do. An explicit deny beats an allow. A role is a set of permissions, not a user.
chapters.leave: MFA, SSO and federation to 6.6; encryption key access to 6.3.

chapters.idea: MFA strengthens one login, SSO reduces repeated logins, and federation lets one trusted identity provider vouch for a user across cloud services.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover MFA factors: knowledge, possession and inherence. Include TOTP, push and FIDO. Explain SSO with SAML and OpenID Connect, the identity provider (IdP), service provider (SP), claims and trust. Mention risks: session theft, misconfigured trust and a single point of failure.

figure.aria: A sequence where a user logs in to one identity provider with a six-digit OTP, and the provider sends signed assertions to three SaaS applications.

chapters.example: A user opens 3 SaaS apps that trust one IdP. Without SSO, that is 3 passwords. With SSO, there is 1 login plus one 6-digit OTP, then 3 signed assertions. If the session lasts 8 hours, how many OTP entries are needed in an 8-hour day? One.
chapters.trap: SSO is not MFA. OAuth 2.0 is for authorization; OpenID Connect adds authentication. Federation trusts the IdP, so a compromised IdP compromises every app that trusts it.
chapters.leave: Detailed IAM policy to 6.5; API security to 6.8.

chapters.idea: A hypervisor isolates VMs, but shared hardware, management planes, images and migration paths mean isolation must be designed and tested.
chapters.depth: Cover VM security across image hardening, patching, guest OS, hypervisor patching, least privilege, VM escape, co-residency, snapshots, cloning and migration. Explain secure isolation strategies, inter-tenant network segmentation and virtualization strategies. Mention containers only as another isolation boundary.

figure.title: Tenant isolation
figure.aria: A host runs a hypervisor with VM A on tenant segment 10.1.0.0/24 and VM B on tenant segment 10.2.0.0/24; traffic between the segments is denied.

chapters.example: A host runs VM A for tenant A on 10.1.0.0/24 and VM B for tenant B on 10.2.0.0/24. A rule allows only TCP 443 from A-web to A-db. All A-to-B traffic is denied. If an attacker on VM A tries 10.2.0.5:22, what happens? The inter-tenant rule denies it.
chapters.trap: VM isolation is not a firewall; two VMs on one host still need network policy. A snapshot can contain credentials and secrets. Migration traffic must be protected.
chapters.leave: Container isolation to Unit 3; network protocols to Unit 2; monitoring to 6.9.

chapters.idea: Cloud bursting and secure interfaces are design patterns that keep identity, data and traffic controlled when a workload crosses a trust boundary.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover burst triggers, a broker, secure tunnel, federated identity, encrypted data and egress rules. For secure interfaces, cover API gateway, mutual TLS, OAuth scopes, input validation and rate limits. Keep the treatment short.

figure.title: Burst split
figure.aria: A peak load of 150 requests per second reaches a burst broker, which sends 100 requests per second to a private cloud and 50 to a public cloud.

chapters.example: A private cloud handles 100 requests/s. A cricket final pushes peak load to 150 requests/s for 2 hours. Burst 50 requests/s to a public cloud. How many requests go public? 50 × 7,200 s = 360,000 requests. At ₹0.001 per request, the burst cost is ₹360.
chapters.trap: Bursting without federated identity and encrypted data leaks tenant data. An API key in a mobile app is not a secure interface. TLS protects transit, not authorization.
chapters.leave: Autoscaling mechanics to Unit 2; API design to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Monitoring gives evidence, auditing proves control, and incident response limits damage in a repeatable loop.
chapters.depth: Cover logs, metrics and traces; cloud audit trails; SIEM; time synchronization and alerting. Explain incident response phases: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover and lessons. Include evidence preservation, provider versus customer logs, and SLA reporting.

figure.aria: An incident response timeline in minutes: detect from 0 to 10, contain from 10 to 30, eradicate from 30 to 90, and recover from 90 to 180.

chapters.example: An incident starts at 09:00. An alert fires at 09:10, the incident is contained at 09:30, and service is recovered at 12:00. Find detection time, containment time and total downtime. Detection = 10 min. Containment = 30 min. Downtime = 180 min = 3 h.
chapters.trap: Logs without synchronized clocks and retention prove little. MTTR is not MTTD. Containment is not recovery.
chapters.leave: Business continuity and fault tolerance to Unit 4; specific SIEM products are out of scope.
